claims.text: Increasing heterogeneous lattice distortion shifts dislocation activity in refractory high-entropy alloys from conventional screw-dominated slip toward edge-dominated mechanisms.
Thermally activated super-jog formation is an example of the proposed edge-dominated mechanism.
The distortion-induced change in dislocation activity preserves yield strength at high temperature.
The proposed change in dislocation activity alters the alloy's thermoelastic response at high temperature.
The relevant initial material is a single-phase refractory high-entropy alloy with significant intrinsic lattice distortion.
Cold rolling followed by annealing, or compositional optimization, can retain significant intrinsic lattice distortion in such an alloy.
Spatial variations in lattice strain affect dislocation core structure.
Spatial variations in lattice strain lead to a prevalence of edge dislocations carrying super-jogs or kinks.
Enhanced heterogeneous lattice distortion creates localized energy barriers that hinder conventional screw-dislocation motion.
Enhanced heterogeneous lattice distortion favors thermally activated edge-dislocation mobility.
The proposed edge-dislocation mechanism mitigates thermal softening and produces a high-temperature yield-strength plateau.
Reducing heterogeneous lattice distortion restores conventional thermally activated dislocation motion and continuous thermal softening.
Relative to a low-distortion baseline, the high-distortion variant will show a significantly smaller decline in yield strength with increasing temperature, potentially forming a plateau.
The high-distortion variant will show more edge-dislocation features than the low-distortion baseline.
A refractory high-entropy alloy engineered for minimal heterogeneous lattice distortion will show a conventional monotonic decrease in yield strength during heating.
Thermal softening is normally expected as temperature rises because dislocation motion becomes easier.
The proposed behavior applies approximately from 600 K to 1073 K when oxidation is suppressed and dislocation-mediated deformation is the primary mechanism.
The two comparison series can differ only in lattice distortion even when that difference is produced through compositional modification or altered processing.
Failure to observe both reduced thermal softening and increased edge-dislocation features in the high-distortion variant would falsify the proposed mechanism.
